source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's NVA4 campus in Sterling, Virginia publishes 11 MW of IT capacity, a modest figure in the largest data center market in the world.

The published specifications cover capacity and technical space only. At 128,715 square feet of technical space loaded to 11 MW, the implied density is about 85 watts per square foot, a plausible figure for mixed colocation rather than a purpose-built AI training hall. CyrusOne publishes no certifications, no address, no rack count, no accelerator count, and no tenant. The record is a capacity number and a facility code, nothing more.

Virginia has 376 mapped data center facilities, and only 29 of them publish a megawatt figure. NVA4 ranks 26th by published capacity among those 29, against a published state total of 2,563.4 MW. The gap between 376 mapped sites and 29 published figures is the more useful fact: most of the state's footprint is invisible in capacity terms, so any state total drawn from published specs is a floor, not a measurement.

For AI scaling, the grid is the binding constraint, and an 11 MW campus is a small increment against a 2,563.4 MW published state total. What this data cannot say is how much capacity Virginia actually holds, how much of it is contracted to AI workloads, or whether NVA4 itself serves any. It establishes one verified data point in a market where verified data points are scarce.
